blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Today `calculateTax` and `calculateCommission` both return `amount * 0.10`. Per this page, what should decide whether the two become a single method?

options.text: Whether a change to one business rule must always change the other
options.says: The page's key question is whether, if one changes, the other must change too.

options.text: Whether the two bodies match each other character for character
options.says: The page says identical-looking code for different domain rules is not a DRY violation.

options.text: Whether the two declarations sit together inside one source file
options.says: The page decides by the knowledge encoded, and says nothing makes placement the test.

questions.stem: A formatting snippet has just appeared for the second time. What does the page's Rule of Three advise?

options.text: Extract a shared method now, before any further copy can appear
options.says: The page says the second time you note the similarity but tolerate it.

options.text: Note the similarity, and keep both copies until another one appears
options.says: The page says: second time, note the similarity but tolerate it; third time, refactor.

options.text: Merge both copies into a generic class with several type parameters
options.says: The page warns against a GenericProcessor<T,R,S,U> after seeing two similar methods.

concepts: DRY is about knowledge, not syntax: two fragments that look alike but encode different rules stay separate, and the test is whether a change to one must change the other.
The Rule of Three waits for a third copy before abstracting, because a premature abstraction can cost more than the duplication.
